subject: Strength of Materials
source: NPTEL / IIT Madras — Prof. K. Ramesh, 40-lecture course (transcripts in ../transcripts/)
goal: Given a slender member under combined torsion + bending + axial load, write the stress tensor at the worst point and decide whether it survives.
learner_prior: Coming in cold on statics, calculus and linear algebra. Rung 0 builds the statics prior from scratch; calculus is taught just-in-time; Mohr's circle substitutes for eigenvectors.

cruxes.title: The Cut
cruxes.hook: You cannot see inside a solid body. So pretend to slice it — and equilibrium of the leftover piece tells you exactly what the inside is doing.
cruxes.owns: Holding a rope that isn't moving: you are pulling exactly as hard as the wall is.
cruxes.payoff: A cross-section transmits exactly six numbers — 3 forces, 3 moments — and nothing else. Axial-force, shear-force, bending-moment and twisting-moment diagrams; the worst cross-section.

cruxes.title: Why the chalk knows which plane to break on
cruxes.hook: Chalk pulled apart snaps flat. The same chalk twisted snaps on a 45° helix. The chalk is not smart — so 'force ÷ area' cannot be the whole story.
cruxes.owns: The cut (rung 0): six numbers on a cross-section.
cruxes.payoff: The stress vector, Cauchy's discovery that three planes pin down all infinitely many, and the stress tensor.

cruxes.title: The circle
cruxes.hook: Rotate the plane you're asking about, and the pair (σ, τ) traces a perfect circle. Why a circle?
cruxes.payoff: Principal stresses, why max shear sits at 45° to max tension — and the retroactive explanation of the chalk.

cruxes.title: The bridge: strain, and one tension test
cruxes.hook: Statics alone cannot tell you the stress. Two equations, three unknowns. You have to ask the material.
cruxes.payoff: Strain as a tensor, σ = Eε, δ = PL/AE, and why two constants characterize an entire isotropic material — down from a possible 21.

cruxes.title: The recipe: guess the deformation, and the stress falls out
cruxes.hook: This subject dodges differential equations by cheating — it conjectures how the body deforms, then checks the guess against experiment.
cruxes.owns: Strain, Hooke's law, and the cut (rungs 0–3).
cruxes.payoff: Kinematics → strain → Hooke → stress → integrate over the area. Torsion formula T/J = τ/r = Gφ/L. Then the learner derives the flexure formula M/I = σ/y = E/ρ unaided.

cruxes.title: The subtle one: shear in beams
cruxes.hook: Stack four loose planks and bend them: the ends fan out like a deck of cards. Glue them and they don't. What is the glue doing?
cruxes.owns: The recipe and the flexure formula (rung 4).
cruxes.payoff: τ = VQ/Ib, from an argument the recipe cannot produce — plus honest limits, shear centre, and why the web of an I-beam exists.

cruxes.title: Deflection
cruxes.hook: The flexure formula already contains the shape of the bent beam — hidden inside the 1/ρ nobody looks at.
cruxes.payoff: EI·d²v/dx² = M, superposition, moment-area, Castigliano — and the key into statically indeterminate problems.

cruxes.title: When does it break?
cruxes.hook: A tension test hands you one number. A real part has three principal stresses. Something must collapse three numbers into one.
cruxes.owns: Principal stresses (rung 2) and the tension test (rung 3).
cruxes.payoff: Tresca, von Mises, Mohr's theory for brittle materials, factor of safety — and sizing a real shaft under combined loading.

cruxes.title: Buckling: where the undeformed shape lies to you
cruxes.hook: Every result so far was computed on the shape the body had BEFORE loading. For a column in compression, that assumption predicts it never fails.
cruxes.payoff: Euler's critical load, effective length, and why buckling is a failure mode anywhere compression exists — not just in columns.
